canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $O$ is given by

$$
z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2},
$$

and a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

Thus, our equation is a hyperbolic paraboloid with the following parameters:

$$
(x_0,y_0,z_0) = (3, -2, 1), \quad a= b=2.
$$

Example: 
                    Identifying Quadric Surfaces by Completing the Square
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square in the $x$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2x+y & =0 \\ -({x}^{2}-2x)+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}-(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-y-1 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =y+1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1, -1, 0).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The most common quadric surfaces are those centered at the origin. We describe these common surfaces in the table below.

| Surface | Equation | Image |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ellipsoid | $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}+\dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/09dc100248a28a5518bcd8428368edefc7c3ee8d5ef0e50515cb7552ee54a376.png) |
| Elliptic Paraboloid | $z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/76e4ad8cb1e83eadae4dce865e100c9a716f9830e7f12adb367b2a9b74d1a651.png) |
| Hyperbolic Paraboloid | $z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/cbc04d7f98e1bb7ce0d62eda71102a6abad708dfcedd7aabee8fff23281471dd.png) |
| Hyperboloid of One Sheet | $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}-\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/df6ef914bc78e121d75baf9f5147784d0e6e434d76800eff60dcb3c3d764477c.png) |
| Hyperboloid of Two Sheets | $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}-\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=-1$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/0870b95c5ce1133d6645e3063174157e36c4354df370c05e48218111ea714838.png) |
| Elliptic Cone | $\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$ | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251512/assets/0f492bf07e573ec7858977e48fa4bf81635e61520b5caa9edef14bd259184347.png) |

Also, recall the following from previous lessons:

- We can generate paraboloids, hyperboloids, and cones with alternative orientation axes by permuting the variables in the corresponding equation. 

For example, the equation of an elliptic cone with its vertex at $O$ and axis of symmetry along the $y$-axis is given by

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.
$$

- We can shift the center/vertex/saddle point of a quadric surface to $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ using the usual coordinate transformation:

$$
(x,y,z) \longrightarrow (x-x_0,y-y_0,z-z_0)
$$

Finally, there is a simple way to distinguish between hyperboloids with one and two sheets by simply looking at the equations:

- *one* minus sign indicates hyperboloids of *one* sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1
$$

- *two* minus signs indicate hyperboloids of *two* sheets:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-}1
$$
